opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most underappreciated aspects of the whole multi-agent discussion. People get excited about the idea of having several agents collaborating, one planning, one writing code, one checking the output, and conceptually that's appealing. But in practice, the reliability of each individual model compounds.

If you have a single LLM call that's, say, 90% reliable on a given step, that sounds pretty good. But if you chain five or ten of those steps together, and each one depends on the previous one being correct, the overall success rate drops off quite quickly. It's basically multiplying probabilities. So a system that looks impressive in a demo can be quite brittle once you run it on many real-world tasks.

There's also the issue that errors don't always stay contained. If one agent hallucinates a function name or misreads a requirement, the downstream agents often take that as a given and build on top of it. Sometimes the mistake gets amplified rather than corrected. You can add a verifier or critic agent, and that does help, but that agent is also an LLM with its own failure modes. In some cases models are too agreeable, so they'll approve something that looks plausible.

So my general take is that improving the base model is still one of the highest-leverage things you can do. A stronger, more consistent individual model makes everything on top of it simpler. And practically, I'd encourage people to start with the simplest setup that works, maybe a single model with good tools and a clear prompt, and only add more agents when there's a clear benefit. Where you can, put in deterministic checks, like running unit tests, validating outputs against a schema, or using a calculator, rather than relying on another LLM to judge correctness. Those grounded signals break the compounding error problem much better than adding more LLMs talking to each other.

That said, I do think multi-agent setups can be really useful, especially when tasks decompose nicely and each subtask is verifiable. But reliability at the individual level is the foundation. If that's shaky, the whole structure on top of it is shaky too.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's actually one of the more underappreciated aspects of multi-agent systems right now. The intuition a lot of people have is that if you take several LLMs and let them collaborate, you get something that's more robust than any single model. And sometimes that's true. But the flip side is that errors compound. If each agent in a pipeline has, let's say, a ten percent chance of making a mistake on a given step, and you chain five or six of those steps together, your end-to-end success rate drops pretty quickly. It's basically a probability multiplication problem.

So the reliability of the individual component really sets a ceiling on what the system can do. I sometimes compare it to building a software system out of unreliable functions. You can add retries, you can add validation layers, you can have a second agent check the first agent's work, but all of that is scaffolding to compensate for the base model not being dependable enough. And that scaffolding costs you latency, it costs you tokens, and it adds complexity that itself can fail.

Where I think the multi-agent approach genuinely helps is when the agents are doing different kinds of things, so their errors aren't correlated. If you have one model drafting code and another one running tests and reporting results, the second agent isn't going to hallucinate in the same way the first one did, because it's grounded in actual tool output. That's very different from having three copies of the same model vote on an answer, where if the model has a systematic blind spot, all three share it. Majority voting doesn't fix correlated errors.

The other thing I'd mention is that reliability isn't just about accuracy on individual answers. It's also about things like instruction following and consistency of output format. In a multi-agent setup, one agent's output becomes another agent's input. If the first model occasionally returns something in a slightly different structure, or adds a bit of commentary where you expected just JSON, the downstream agent might handle that unpredictably. Those are the kinds of failures that are hard to catch in a demo but show up constantly in production.

So my honest take is that the individual model reliability is probably the single biggest lever. A lot of the multi-agent research results you see are partly a reflection of the base models getting better, and I think people sometimes attribute to the architecture what really came from the underlying model. If you gave me a choice between a clever orchestration scheme on top of mediocre models, or a simple pipeline on top of really reliable ones, I'd pick the second one almost every time.

r002.rationale: It explains that errors compound when steps are chained and that one agent’s output becomes another’s input, reducing end-to-end success as more dependent steps are added.

r003.rationale: It calls individual model reliability the “single biggest lever” and favors improving the underlying models over relying on clever orchestration.

astra-6.text:
I think the reliability of the individual models is really the foundation. If a model struggles to do a task reliably, putting several copies of it into a multi-agent system doesn’t automatically solve that problem. You can actually compound the errors, especially when one agent’s output becomes the input to the next agent. That next agent might take a mistaken assumption as a fact and build on it.

There is an opportunity to improve reliability by having agents check each other’s work, but the key question is whether those checks are meaningful. If they all use the same model and have similar failure modes, they can agree and still be wrong. Agreement alone isn’t verification.

So I would start with a strong single-model baseline, then add agents where there’s a clear benefit—perhaps dividing a task into narrower responsibilities or checking an output against something testable. And ultimately, you have to measure whether that whole system is actually more reliable. Having more agents isn’t, by itself, evidence that it is.

r002.rationale: It says errors can compound when one agent depends on another’s output, but does not state that adding mutually dependent LLMs increases the risk that at least one will fail.

r003.rationale: It calls individual-model reliability foundational and recommends starting with a strong single-model baseline, but does not identify improving the underlying LLMs as the primary way to improve multi-agent performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reliability of the individual models is really the foundation. If an agent makes a mistake and passes that result to another agent, the next agent may just accept it and build on it. So adding more agents doesn’t automatically make the system more reliable. You can also end up compounding errors.

Where multiple agents can help is if you have a way to check the work. For example, one agent proposes a solution, another critiques it, and then you verify the result with something concrete, like running code or tests. But if all the agents are using the same model, they may share the same blind spots. Agreement alone isn’t necessarily evidence that they’re correct.

So I would start with a strong single-agent baseline and ask what each additional agent contributes. Does it provide independent information or a useful verification step? And does that improvement justify the additional cost and complexity? I think that’s more important than the number of agents.
